claims.text: The hypothesis applies to CrFeCoNiX alloys, where X is Si, Mn, or Al, in single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution states.
Above 900 °C, a stable and coherent oxide scale forms when alloy composition promotes preferential surface enrichment of Cr or Al.
The protective scale is predominantly Cr2O3, or Al2O3 when Al is present.
Al2O3 is a slower-growing and more stable high-temperature protective oxide than Cr2O3.
The proposed oxide scale grows under diffusion control.
The protective scale limits inward oxygen transport while growth occurs predominantly through outward cation migration.
Cr diffuses outward faster than oxygen diffuses inward, so chromia scales usually grow outward.
A sufficiently large outward flux of an active element relative to the inward oxygen flux favors formation of an external protective oxide.
Maintaining a continuous, slowly thickening scale causes the oxide to remain coherent and protective.
An excessively large mismatch between metal-cation and oxygen diffusivities generates localized stresses that cause scale cracking or spallation.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between an oxide scale and its substrate can cause cracking and spallation during thermal cycling.
Sufficient Cr or Al surface enrichment will produce a slow-growing scale that resists cracking and spallation.
Limited Cr or Al surface enrichment will cause accelerated scale growth and internal stress.
Limited Cr or Al surface enrichment will eventually lead to cracking or spallation.
An equimolar CrFeCoNiX alloy without deliberately enhanced segregation effects can serve as the comparison baseline.
The mechanism is intended to apply in both oxidative and corrosive atmospheres above 900 °C.
Microstructure, surface heterogeneity, and high-temperature phase instability can make oxide structures highly variable in multicomponent HEAs.
Failure of measured segregation or diffusion profiles to correlate with protective-scale formation would falsify the proposed mechanism.
